body.en: Every method so far — characteristic equations, undetermined coefficients, variation of parameters, Laplace transforms — needs constant coefficients. The moment an equation has a variable coefficient, like \( y''-xy'-y=0 \), none of them apply. This chapter's method needs no such restriction: assume the solution is a power series with unknown coefficients, substitute into the ODE, and read off a recurrence relation the coefficients must satisfy.

label.en: ● Definition 8.1 — Ordinary point; power series solution

body.en: For \( y''+P(x)y'+Q(x)y=0 \), a point \( x_0 \) is an ordinary point if \( P,Q \) are both analytic (equal to their own convergent power series) at \( x_0 \) — every polynomial coefficient qualifies everywhere. At an ordinary point, seek a solution of the form \[ y=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-x_0)^n, \] substitute into the ODE, collect like powers of \( (x-x_0) \), and set each coefficient to zero — this produces a recurrence relation expressing \( a_{n+2} \) (or whichever index the algebra produces) in terms of earlier coefficients. The two free parameters \( a_0=y(x_0) \) and \( a_1=y'(x_0) \) then play the same role Chapter 3's two constants \( C_1,C_2 \) did.

Find a power series solution of \( y''-xy'-y=0 \) about \( x_0=0 \).

Let \( y=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n \), so \( y'=\sum_{n=1}^\infty na_nx^{n-1} \) and \( y''=\sum_{n=2}^\infty n(n-1)a_nx^{n-2} \). Substitute:

\[ \sum_{n=2}^\infty n(n-1)a_nx^{n-2}-x\sum_{n=1}^\infty na_nx^{n-1}-\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n=0. \]

Shift the first sum's index (\( m=n-2 \)) so every sum is indexed by the same power \( x^n \): \[ \sum_{n=0}^\infty(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}x^n-\sum_{n=1}^\infty na_nx^n-\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n=0. \] The middle sum's missing \( n=0 \) term is \( 0 \) anyway (its coefficient is \( 0\cdot a_0 \)), so every sum can start at \( n=0 \); the coefficient of \( x^n \) must vanish for every \( n\ge0 \): \[ (n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}-na_n-a_n=0\;\Longrightarrow\;a_{n+2}=\frac{a_n}{n+2}. \]

Even coefficients (from \( a_0 \)): \( a_2=\dfrac{a_0}{2} \), \( a_4=\dfrac{a_2}{4}=\dfrac{a_0}{8} \), \( a_6=\dfrac{a_4}{6}=\dfrac{a_0}{48} \) — in general \( a_{2k}=\dfrac{a_0}{2^kk!} \), giving \[ y_1(x)=a_0\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(x^2/2)^k}{k!}=a_0\,e^{x^2/2}. \] (Check directly: \( y_1=e^{x^2/2}\Rightarrow y_1'=xe^{x^2/2}\Rightarrow y_1''=e^{x^2/2}+x^2e^{x^2/2} \), and \( y_1''-xy_1'-y_1=e^{x^2/2}+x^2e^{x^2/2}-x^2e^{x^2/2}-e^{x^2/2}=0 \). ✓ — the series resums to a genuine elementary function.)

Odd coefficients (from \( a_1 \)): \( a_3=\dfrac{a_1}{3} \), \( a_5=\dfrac{a_3}{5}=\dfrac{a_1}{15} \), \( a_7=\dfrac{a_5}{7}=\dfrac{a_1}{105} \), giving the second, independent solution \[ y_2(x)=a_1\Big(x+\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{x^5}{15}+\frac{x^7}{105}+\cdots\Big) — \] a genuine power series that does not resum to any elementary function, which is the entire point of this method: it produces a valid solution even when Chapters 3–5's closed forms simply don't exist.

General solution: \( y=y_1+y_2 \), i.e. \( a_0e^{x^2/2}+a_1\big(x+\tfrac{x^3}{3}+\tfrac{x^5}{15}+\cdots\big) \), with \( a_0=y(0) \), \( a_1=y'(0) \).

At an ordinary point \( x_0 \), taking \( (a_0,a_1)=(1,0) \) gives one solution \( y_1 \) and \( (a_0,a_1)=(0,1) \) gives another, \( y_2 \); since \( y_1(x_0)=1,\,y_1'(x_0)=0 \) while \( y_2(x_0)=0,\,y_2'(x_0)=1 \), neither is a constant multiple of the other, so they're linearly independent and \( y=C_1y_1+C_2y_2 \) is the general solution — both constants doing exactly the job \( C_1,C_2 \) did in Chapter 3, for any ordinary-point equation, not just this chapter's examples.

What is not true in general is that this \( a_0 \)/\( a_1 \) split always lines up with a clean even/odd split of the coefficients: that extra decoupling is special to a recurrence like Worked example 8.A's \( a_{n+2}=a_n/(n+2) \), which relates \( a_{n+2} \) only to \( a_n \) (skipping \( a_{n+1} \) entirely) — exactly the shape that keeps every even-indexed coefficient depending only on \( a_0 \) and every odd-indexed one only on \( a_1 \). A three-term recurrence relating \( a_{n+2} \) to both \( a_{n+1} \) and \( a_n \) (which a less symmetric coefficient function can produce) still yields two independent solutions this same way, just without that particular even/odd bookkeeping shortcut.

label.en: Worked example 8.B — Recovering a known equation

body.en:
Solve \( y''+y=0 \) by power series, and check the answer against Chapter 3's characteristic-equation method.

\( y=\sum a_nx^n \Rightarrow\sum(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}x^n+\sum a_nx^n=0\Rightarrow a_{n+2}=\dfrac{-a_n}{(n+2)(n+1)}. \)

Even: \( a_2=-\dfrac{a_0}{2},\,a_4=\dfrac{a_0}{24},\ldots \) — the pattern is \( a_{2k}=\dfrac{(-1)^ka_0}{(2k)!} \), so \( y_1=a_0\sum\dfrac{(-1)^kx^{2k}}{(2k)!}=a_0\cos x \). Odd: identically, \( y_2=a_1\sin x \).

General solution \( y=C_1\cos x+C_2\sin x \) — exactly Chapter 3, Theorem 3.2's complex-root case for \( r^2+1=0 \) (\( \alpha=0,\beta=1 \)), confirming the series method reduces to the old method whenever the old method already applied.

value.en: Substitute, shift indices to match powers of \( x \), set each coefficient to 0
One from \( a_0 \) (with \( a_1=0 \)), one from \( a_1 \) (with \( a_0=0 \))

body.en:
Find the recurrence relation for a power series solution of \( y'-2xy=0 \) about \( x_0=0 \), and identify the resulting closed form.

Show solution

\( y=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n\Rightarrow y'=\sum_{n=1}^\infty na_nx^{n-1}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty(n+1)a_{n+1}x^n \) (reindexing). And \( 2xy=2\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^{n+1}=2\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{n-1}x^n \) — this one starts at \( n=1 \), not \( n=0 \), since shifting \( x^{n+1} \) to \( x^n \) shifts the starting index up by one.

So \[ \sum_{n=0}^\infty(n+1)a_{n+1}x^n-2\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{n-1}x^n=0. \] At \( n=0 \), only the first sum contributes: \( a_1=0 \). For \( n\ge1 \): \( (n+1)a_{n+1}=2a_{n-1}\Rightarrow a_{n+1}=\dfrac{2a_{n-1}}{n+1} \).

Iterating from \( a_0 \) (with \( a_1=0 \) forcing every odd-indexed coefficient to \( 0 \)): \( a_2=\dfrac{2a_0}{2}=a_0,\,a_3=\dfrac{2a_1}{3}=0,\,a_4=\dfrac{2a_2}{4}=\dfrac{a_0}{2},\,a_5=0,\,a_6=\dfrac{2a_4}{6}=\dfrac{a_0}{6} \) — matching \( a_{2k}=a_0/k! \), so \( y=a_0\sum_{k=0}^\infty\dfrac{x^{2k}}{k!}=a_0e^{x^2} \). \( y=a_0e^{x^2} \) — confirmed directly, since \( y'=2xa_0e^{x^2}=2xy \). ✓

label.en: First few terms of a series solution

body.en:
Find the first four nonzero terms of the series solution of \( y''-xy=0 \) (Airy's equation) with \( y(0)=1,\,y'(0)=0 \).

Solution: \( \sum(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}x^n=x\sum a_nx^n=\sum a_nx^{n+1} \). Matching powers: \( a_2=0 \) (no \( x^0 \) term on the right), and for \( n\ge1 \), \( (n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}=a_{n-1} \).

With \( a_0=1,\,a_1=0,\,a_2=0 \): \( a_3=\dfrac{a_0}{3\cdot2}=\dfrac16 \), \( a_4=\dfrac{a_1}{4\cdot3}=0 \), \( a_5=\dfrac{a_2}{5\cdot4}=0 \), \( a_6=\dfrac{a_3}{6\cdot5}=\dfrac{1}{180} \). So \( y\approx1+\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dfrac{x^6}{180}+\cdots \)

Explain why \( y_1=e^{x^2/2} \) and \( y_2=x+\tfrac{x^3}{3}+\tfrac{x^5}{15}+\cdots \) from Worked example 8.A are linearly independent, without computing a Wronskian.

Solution: \( y_1(0)=1\neq0 \) but \( y_2(0)=0 \) — if \( y_2=ky_1 \) for a constant \( k \), evaluating at \( x=0 \) gives \( 0=k \), forcing \( y_2\equiv0 \), which is false. So neither is a scalar multiple of the other.

question.en: Practice: Find the recurrence relation for \( y''-y=0 \) using a power series about \( x_0=0 \), and identify \( y_1 \) (from \( a_0=1,a_1=0 \)).

solution.en: \( \sum(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}x^n=\sum a_nx^n\Rightarrow a_{n+2}=\dfrac{a_n}{(n+2)(n+1)} \). With \( a_0=1,a_1=0 \): \( a_2=\frac12,\,a_4=\frac{1}{24},\ldots\), matching \( a_{2k}=1/(2k)! \), so \( y_1=\sum x^{2k}/(2k)!=\cosh x \) — consistent with Chapter 3's real-roots case for \( r^2-1=0\Rightarrow r=\pm1 \).
